title: Bar Review: La Petite Grocery, New Orleans
summary:
More of a neighborhood bistro than a bar, La Petite Grocery has been a fixture in the Uptown district since 2004 — and under its current management since 2010. Chef Justin Devillier won a James Beard Award in 2016 for his upscale New Orleans fare, and having spent an evening here during the recent Tales…

The post Bar Review: La Petite Grocery, New Orleans appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
More of a neighborhood bistro than a bar, La Petite Grocery has been a fixture in the Uptown district since 2004 — and under its current management since 2010. Chef Justin Devillier won a James Beard Award in 2016 for his upscale New Orleans fare, and having spent an evening here during the recent Tales of the Cocktail conference, it’s easy to see why. Massive plates of Cajun delights filled our table — alongside gentle spins on classic cocktails, too.

I’m going to break tradition and talk about the food first, with which I was unable to find much fault. The blue crab beignets are a signature dish here, and the two-bite delights rightfully earn their place as one of NOLA’s most essential single dishes. A short rib appetizer bursts with beefy flavor, and a simply prepared redfish dish felt straight off the boat. As we were dining on a Monday, red beans and rice were on the menu, a massive plate served with cornbread and topped with a showstopping chicken thigh that I couldn’t put down. If you come hungry — and you’ll need to — spending an extra seven bucks on the biggest bowl of French fries in town is the best move you can make.

Of course, we’re here for the drinks, and they didn’t disappoint. We tried four items on the curated cocktail list (all $13 to $18), all classics made with something of a twist.

My favorite was a surprise called the Cassius Club, made with Tito’s vodka, apricot, Steen’s syrup, lemon, and absinthe. I almost never drink vodka cocktails but this refreshing and summery libation was perfect on a blazing hot New Orleans day. The apricot pops without being overwhelming, while the lemon and licorice-laced absinthe make for a seductive finish.

The most unique cocktail in the lineup that I tried was the Bittersweet Motel, a mix of Novo Fogo cachaca, Tempus Fugit banana liqueur, Fernet Paesani, and Bitterman’s Xocolatl Mole Bitters. It sounds wild and it is, and while our server described it as a (loose) riff on a Negroni, it took some mental gymnastics to make that connection. I especially enjoyed this as the ice melted a bit, coaxing the banana flavor from the middle ground to a dominant position on the palate.

More traditional fare included tastes of a Bee’s Knees (Bombay gin, honey, lavender, and lemon), with understated spice and smoldering honey, and the Blood Oath, a pumped-up version of a Blood and Sand, made with Michter’s rye, Cherry Heering, falernum, orange, and lime. It was the only cocktail in the bunch that I felt might be a bit too over the top, its fruit notes becoming overwhelming in the end.

Service here was gracious and extremely friendly, our server taking time to chat through the history of the establishment and a bit of her own journey — all managing to avoid feeling like we were being schooled while sitting in a classroom. I’ll definitely be back.

4238 Magazine St, New Orleans, LA 70115
lapetitegrocery.com

title: Review: Mount Gay Exceptionally Aged 15 Years Old and 25 Years Old
summary:
Barbados’ Mount Gay surprised us recently with the launch of a new rum collection: Exceptionally Aged. As you can imagine, the focus of these releases will be extended maturation, with the first two offerings hitting 15 and 25 years of age, respectively. Both are aged entirely in ex-bourbon casks at the distillery in Barbados and…

The post Review: Mount Gay Exceptionally Aged 15 Years Old and 25 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Barbados’ Mount Gay surprised us recently with the launch of a new rum collection: Exceptionally Aged. As you can imagine, the focus of these releases will be extended maturation, with the first two offerings hitting 15 and 25 years of age, respectively. Both are aged entirely in ex-bourbon casks at the distillery in Barbados and include no added sugar or flavoring. Three generations of Mount Gay Master Blenders — Jerry Edwards, Allen Smith, and current Master Blender Trudiann Branker — collaborated on these initial releases.

Mount Gay Exceptionally Aged 15 Years Old Review

Even at 15 years of age (all in ex-bourbon casks), this rum hits the nose with exuberant freshness, filled with apple-driven fruit and fully laced with caramel and vanilla. Brown butter notes are insistent and arrive alongside a healthy baking spice complement. There’s so much of it on the nose that this could easily be used as a spiced rum for mixing, assuming your pockets have a bit of extra coin in them.

Things are a bit more austere on the palate, which settles into a slightly winey groove that’s backed up by ample barrel char and overtones of cocoa powder and ground coffee, the spice hitting a bit more savory, with a cardamom quality and a pinch of saffron. An initial rush of sweetness tempers as the finish leans into notes of toasted coconut, grapefruit peel, and red wine. Refined and, in the end, rather mysterious. 4942 bottles produced.

86 proof. A- / $90

Mount Gay Exceptionally Aged 25 Years Old Review

At 25 years of age, things really start to get wild. The nose is shockingly dry — and quite winey, evoking thoughts of sherry even though this rum has no wine cask involvement at all. Austere with overtones of furniture polish and leather, the rum’s aromatic profile soon turns rather ashy, with creosote notes becoming dominant in time.

The palate perks up quickly with notes of coconut, orange, and a light honey character, but this all evaporates almost immediately. Notes of very dark chocolate replace all of the above, leading to a finish that is dry as dust, though some tight notes of toasted coconut and bitter orange peel linger. Has this rum simply sat in the Caribbean heat for too long, burning away all its charm? Those in a better headspace than me may enjoy it, but I really can’t see it any other way except to call this one simply too far gone for easy consumption. 2376 bottles produced.

92 proof. B / $199

title: Review: 2022 Aesthetic Cabernet Sauvignon California
summary:
A “California” designation on a bottle of cabernet sauvignon is usually a kiss of budgety death, but this wine combats expectations from the jump. Aesthetic’s 2022 cab is easily mistakeable for a midrange Napa release, juicy with plums and currants en route to notes of baking spice, dusted with orange peel and touched lightly with…

The post Review: 2022 Aesthetic Cabernet Sauvignon California appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
A “California” designation on a bottle of cabernet sauvignon is usually a kiss of budgety death, but this wine combats expectations from the jump.

Aesthetic’s 2022 cab is easily mistakeable for a midrange Napa release, juicy with plums and currants en route to notes of baking spice, dusted with orange peel and touched lightly with oak. A hint of bay leaf gives the finish a slightly savory bent, though the sweetness of the currant notes wavers only slightly. The finish evokes chocolate sauce, Hershey’s, with a sharp touch of cherry.

A very solid choice for the price.

A- / $40

title: Review: Green River Distillery Select Toasted Double Oak Bourbon
summary:
Bardstown Bourbon Co. has had no shortage of success with their newish Distillery Reserve Series, a collection of consistently impressive and unique whiskeys available exclusively to distillery visitors and members of their whiskey club, The Reserve. Now, their sister distillery in Owensboro, Green River, is getting in on the action with its own exclusive series…

The post Review: Green River Distillery Select Toasted Double Oak Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Bardstown Bourbon Co. has had no shortage of success with their newish Distillery Reserve Series, a collection of consistently impressive and unique whiskeys available exclusively to distillery visitors and members of their whiskey club, The Reserve. Now, their sister distillery in Owensboro, Green River, is getting in on the action with its own exclusive series dubbed Distillery Select.

While Bardstown’s Distillery Reserve Series tends to focus on exotic finishes and blends containing double digit age statement whiskeys, the new Distillery Select Series will reportedly “celebrate straightforward innovations,” meaning more traditional offerings with more modest age statements that will showcase different proofs, classic finishes, and specific rickhouse selections. The price point is also more accessible, coming in at half the cost of Bardstown’s offerings.

That’s not to say these aren’t special whiskeys, as is clear with this debut release. To kick things off, Green River is bottling their oldest bourbon to date, an eight-year-old made from their flagship mashbill of 70% corn, 21% rye, and 9% malted barley. Just thirteen barrels were chosen for the release, each finished for six months in a light char, medium toast new American oak barrel coopered by Independent Stave Company. Thoughts follow.

Green River Distillery Select Toasted Double Oak Bourbon Review

The nose is a bit soft at first, but given time to bloom, it delivers a rich bouquet that’s impressively dynamic. Early notes of Demerara sugar and cocoa powder are light and airy yet suggestive of the darker, richer sweetness to come. Undertones of baked apples and caramelized peach cobbler arrive in short order, adding a fruity depth. As things bloom even further, the fruit gives way to light roast coffee bean, maple candies, and sweet sawdust, all laced with cinnamon syrup. It’s a pleasure just to nose.

On the palate, things are well-spiced right out of the gate with bold notes of black pepper, burnt sugar, clove syrup, and tart black cherry that simmer with a hugging, chili pepper warmth across the sip. The flavors are wood driven to be sure, but they never come across astringent or over-oaked. In fact, this is one of the more balanced double oak expressions I’ve tasted. What few tannins present initially soften completely into the midpalate amid additional notes of Belgian chocolate, dark caramel, split vanilla bean, and a slightly smoky hint of charred marshmallow. The finish is rich and silky, with warm notes of baking spice and chocolate-covered caramels.

This debut Distillery Select release from Green River almost rivals some of the pricier and more exotic distillery-only whiskeys from Bardstown. There’s no club (yet) for these rare whiskeys, so you’ll have to get to Owensboro or Green River’s tasting room in Louisville to sample for yourself.

115.1 proof.

A- / $50

title: Review: Nashville Teas and Lemonades
summary:
TailGate Brewery makes a collection of classic beers, and surprisingly it’s also behind a tea-and-lemonade brand called Nashville (named after its home city). Both tea and lemonade can be useful cocktailing ingredients, so let’s give these canned offerings a shot. All come in massive 16 oz. containers. Nashville Lemonade – If this had had a…

The post Review: Nashville Teas and Lemonades appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
TailGate Brewery makes a collection of classic beers, and surprisingly it’s also behind a tea-and-lemonade brand called Nashville (named after its home city). Both tea and lemonade can be useful cocktailing ingredients, so let’s give these canned offerings a shot. All come in massive 16 oz. containers.

Nashville Lemonade – If this had had a bit of pulp in it, I’d have been convinced it was homemade. Mind you, one can will get you 76% of your recommended daily allowance of sugar, but the tart lemon notes are authentic and crisp, effectively cutting through all that sweetness. It’s for sure a decadent treat on its own, and a useful shortcut for cocktailing as a lemony mixer. A-

Nashville Sunshine – A mix of sweet tea and lemonade — Nashville’s answer to the Arnold Palmer. It’s surprisingly fruity up top, almost like it’s made with Nashville’s peach tea instead of sweet tea, with a squeeze of lemon added to the mix. After the rush of sweet fruit fades, the tea comes into focus — particularly on the expressive nose, once it gets some time in glass. Ultimately the balance between the two halves is pretty spot on, making for a beverage that might be better than the sum of its parts. A-

Nashville Sweet Tea – A moderate to strong sun tea flavor kicks things off — classic and vaguely minty — until a healthy sweetness comes into focus and takes over. Though it’s sweetened just with cane sugar, the character hits as equal parts brown sugar and honey thanks to the interaction with the underlying tea. At 180 calories per can, that sugar is doing an awful lot of the talking — but damn if it doesn’t take you on a trip straight back to Sunday afternoons in the South. B+

Nashville Peach Tea – I’m not really a fan of peach (or really any fruit) in my tea, but for some I know it’s the only way to fly. The flavor is not inauthentic or overloaded, but the extra sweetness is palpable. At 180 calories per can it’s a lot to manage in sugar alone — and the fruit notes become even stronger as the tea warms up. Too much for me. B

each $24 per 12 pack of 16 oz. cans

title: Review: Copper and Kings Revival Brandy and King’s Proof Bourbon (2026)
summary:
As the United States celebrates its 250th anniversary in 2026, consumers have been inundated with bourbon releases commemorating “America 250.” Bourbon is often described as “America’s native spirit,” yet the spirit we recognize today did not exist in 1776. American fruit brandy, however, already had a place in the country’s early distilling tradition. Two and…

The post Review: Copper and Kings Revival Brandy and King’s Proof Bourbon (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
As the United States celebrates its 250th anniversary in 2026, consumers have been inundated with bourbon releases commemorating “America 250.” Bourbon is often described as “America’s native spirit,” yet the spirit we recognize today did not exist in 1776. American fruit brandy, however, already had a place in the country’s early distilling tradition.

Two and a half centuries later, American brandy occupies only a small corner of the domestic spirits market, especially when compared with bourbon. Age is another point of separation. Most American brandy distillers simply do not have inventories capable of matching the age statements commonly found on bourbon labels. Even so, a small group of distillers has released American brandy with significant maturity. While this may not be an absolutely exhaustive list, it comes very close: Laird & Company, Clear Creek, Germain-Robin, Charbay, and Louisville’s Copper & Kings American Brandy Company.

Founded in 2014, Copper & Kings has already experienced several ownership changes, most recently when Rob Bourdon acquired the company in August 2025. Long before that transition, the distillery had established a reputation for turning out excellent American brandy, including the high-proof Butchertown Reserve Casks Brandy, named for the Louisville neighborhood the distillery calls home. In 2023, Copper & Kings also paid tribute to Kentucky’s bourbon heritage with the release of a sourced bourbon blend, each component finished in the distillery’s own apple brandy barrels.

Both Butchertown Reserve Casks Brandy and the original bourbon release predated Bourdon’s ownership. Following the acquisition, the Butchertown name was retired as Bourdon set out to reshape Copper & Kings’ identity with new branding, updated imagery, and a different marketing direction. He also began working with older stocks of aged brandy and bourbon than had been available under Constellation Brands.

The first releases under Bourdon arrived in late 2025 with Copper & Kings VSOP Brandy 6 Years Old, bottled at 86 proof, alongside his version of Copper & Kings Bourbon. Like its predecessor, each bourbon component was finished in Copper & Kings’ apple brandy barrels before bottling at 93 proof.

During the summer of 2026, Bourdon followed those releases with Copper & Kings Revival Brandy, the successor to Butchertown Reserve Casks Brandy, and Copper & Kings King’s Proof Bourbon. Both were bottled at 114.8 proof, a substantial increase over the late-2025 releases. More importantly, these are entirely new blends built from older stocks rather than higher-proof editions of the previous releases.

Copper & Kings had already established a reputation for quality brandy and bourbon before Rob Bourdon took the helm. Now he is building on that foundation with new product development ideas, a different approach to blending, and a fresh direction for the distillery.

Are these two newest releases worthy of your attention? Is Copper & Kings worth watching going forward? Let’s find out.

Copper & Kings Revival American Brandy VSOP 8 Years Old (2026) Review

Batch #1 of Copper & Kings Revival American Brandy VSOP carries an 8-year age statement and marks Rob Bourdon’s first high-proof blending project. The back label states “produced by Copper & Kings,” wording that bourbon drinkers often associate with sourced whiskey. While Copper & Kings has bottled sourced brandy in the past and still has sourced stocks maturing in its warehouses, Revival is blended exclusively from brandy distilled by Copper & Kings in Louisville, Kentucky.

Revival is intended to remain a blend of just four to ten barrels, making every batch its own release rather than an attempt at exact replication. The brandy is distilled from Muscat, Colombard, and Chenin Blanc grapes, with 25% of the blend matured in new charred American oak and the remaining 75% matured in ex-bourbon barrels sourced from several Kentucky distilleries.

The age range spans eight to twelve years, with an average of roughly ten years. Brandy matured in new charred American oak generally falls between eight and ten years old, while the brandy matured in ex-bourbon barrels typically ranges from ten to twelve years, with the twelve-year component making up the smallest share of the blend.

Most of the barrels spent the majority of their maturation period at an off-site warehouse rather than in the Butchertown cellar. They typically began aging in the Butchertown cellar for anywhere from several months to a couple of years before moving to the off-site warehouse, then returned to the Butchertown cellar for several more years before harvest. There is no fixed harvesting season, although releases will generally follow a spring through autumn timetable.

After the selected barrels were blended, the brandy rested for several weeks before bottling. Revival is bottled at 114.8 proof following an undisclosed reduction from its natural harvest proof and contains no added sugar.

The nose opens with a powerful note of dark honeycomb, full of dark honey and beeswax. That opening aroma holds its place before giving way to toasted almonds and sultanas. After a minute in the glass, dusty dried tobacco joins the bouquet, though the honeycomb remains present throughout. There is very little to criticize here. For anyone who appreciates fine brandy, the aroma is exceptionally nice.

Curiously, the prominent honeycomb note from the nose never makes the trip to the palate. Instead, the first sip begins on a sweet note with candied pineapple, stewed apricots, and baked pears dusted with cinnamon, delivering plenty of juicy fruit. The midpoint then shifts dramatically. Dry leather arrives without warning, and the fruit never returns. Bitter orange peel steps forward before yielding to dusty limestone and dried mint leaf, while baked red apple peel closes everything out.

From beginning to end, this is an outstanding brandy. Revival surpasses every previous edition of Butchertown. Earlier releases offered plenty to enjoy, but they also possessed a certain roughness that is entirely absent here, making Revival a far more complete pour. It belongs in the conversation with the greatest American brandies released to date, regardless of distillery. Based purely on enjoyment, Revival may well be the greatest American grape brandy I’ve tasted. Oregon’s Clear Creek 15 Year Old Apple Brandy stands on the same level, though it comes from apples rather than grapes.

In early 2026, I traveled to Copper & Kings to select a single barrel, tasting ten exceptional cask strength brandies along the way. Every one of those barrels impressed at full proof, yet every one improved with a small addition of water while remaining at a high proof. None ultimately showed its best at true cask strength. Bottled below full cask strength while still maintaining plenty of proof, Revival follows that same pattern, showcasing brandy at what I believe is its peak rather than chasing maximum proof for its own sake. 114.8 proof. A / $65

Copper & Kings King’s Proof Bourbon Finished in Brandy Barrels (2026) Review

King’s Proof is built from a blend of four to eight barrels, each finished in Copper & Kings apple brandy barrels for periods ranging from one to three years. Before being used for secondary maturation, the casks had held apple brandy for roughly seven years.

The largest component, representing 65% of the blend, was distilled by Bardstown Bourbon Company and matured for five years before entering the apple brandy casks. Another 24% comes from an undisclosed Bardstown distillery and was distilled from a mashbill of 78% corn, 10% rye, and 12% malted barley. That whiskey spent ten years maturing before its apple brandy cask finish. The remaining 12% was distilled at another undisclosed Bardstown distillery from a mashbill of 74% corn, 18% rye, and 8% malted barley, then matured for fifteen years before secondary maturation.

Although Bourdon disclosed that the various blend components spent anywhere from one to three years in apple brandy casks, he did not specify which whiskeys received the longest finishing periods. In late 2025, Copper & Kings released a single barrel bourbon distilled in Bardstown from the same 74% corn, 18% rye, and 8% malted barley mashbill. That whiskey spent fifteen years maturing before receiving an apple brandy cask finish that extended beyond three years. While there is no confirmation, it is not unreasonable to assume that King’s Proof could also include fifteen-year-old Bardstown-distilled bourbon finished in apple brandy casks for three years.

One notable difference separates King’s Proof from Batch #1 of Copper & Kings Bourbon. Bourdon’s 2025 bourbon release included a ten-year-old component distilled by an undisclosed distillery in central Kentucky. In a move that hopefully won’t ruffle too many tail feathers, King’s Proof does not include any stock from that distillery, setting the two blends apart in ways that extend well beyond their respective proofs.

Like Revival, King’s Proof is bottled at 114.8 proof after an undisclosed reduction from the blend’s natural harvest proof, while remaining at a proof point likely to please experienced imbiber.

Bourdon also notes that nearly every finished bourbon barrel at Copper & Kings spent its entire maturation period in the Butchertown cellar, with only a small number aging at the off-site warehouse. As with the brandy, every bourbon barrel also underwent Copper & Kings’ sonic aging program, and each one spent time listening to the Grateful Dead.

The influence of the apple brandy casks stands out immediately, with baked apples leading the aroma from the first nosing. Cinnamon stick follows alongside it, offering an earthier profile than ground cinnamon. Toasted almonds and brown sugar add to the bouquet, and after the glass has had ample time to rest, old leather arrives. The apple brandy influence remains consistent throughout, and although these barrels account for the smaller portion of the blend, the well-aged whiskey makes a strong showing without becoming overly tannic. Even if roughly 65% of the blend only spent somewhere beyond six years in oak, the apple brandy finishing gives the bourbon an aroma that consistently suggests greater maturity than its youngest components would indicate.

The palate opens with oxidized apples and cardamom before the apple brandy casks continue to shape the whiskey through the arrival of chamomile and a touch of peppermint across the midpalate. Viscosity lands slightly above medium, though it stops short of becoming especially thick.

The finish changes direction in a surprising way. Dry-roasted, lightly salted peanuts combine with dried apple chips, creating an effect much like county fair caramel apples coated with chopped peanuts. Eucalyptus makes a brief appearance before pink peppercorn bursts forward for one final statement. That pink peppercorn note lasts an exceptionally long time and finishes with a lot of spice, steering the bourbon away from everything that came before it. The spice is just enough out of proportion to trim a little of the shine from what is otherwise a highly cohesive sipping experience.

Between the originality of the apple brandy finish, the proof, the price, and the age, this is an easy bottle to recommend and one that is unlikely to leave anyone disappointed. Rob Bourdon is off to an excellent start as a blender, and I look forward to seeing where future releases go. 114.8 proof. A- / $65

title: Review: The Gin Edit and Soda Shoppe Recipe Card Decks
summary:
I’ve spent an unreasonable number of words whining about “having a moment,” a phrase so thoroughly worn out by the spirits world that it now arrives exhausted: nothing more than a fishing anecdote now in its twenty-fifth year of an endless morphing and recitation. However, it seems that recipe cards are generously enjoying a glint,…

The post Review: The Gin Edit and Soda Shoppe Recipe Card Decks appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
I’ve spent an unreasonable number of words whining about “having a moment,” a phrase so thoroughly worn out by the spirits world that it now arrives exhausted: nothing more than a fishing anecdote now in its twenty-fifth year of an endless morphing and recitation. However, it seems that recipe cards are generously enjoying a glint, possibly a flicker, if the lighting’s right. I will not be talked into more than that. Last month, rum and no/low-alcohol cards were under review. This month, we pivot to two fresh decks: gin cocktails on one side, soda fountain recipes on the other, both asking nothing of you but modest ambition.

Soda Shoppe Recipe Cards – First up is Soda Shoppe, a deck of 50 cards devoted to the bygone Boomer era where malt and soda shoppes were a major social meeting point for the teens of the time. Designed with the nostalgic Americana in mind, the cards are divided into several categories: retro, fruity, floats, dirty sodas, international and, somewhat wildly, a whole eight cards devoted to egg creams. There are many familiar classics but also some new ones that may pique the interest of those looking for something different, and most of the recipes (save for the Matcha soda) are relatively straightforward. A nice one to have around when it’s a family night in, or alcohol isn’t in the cards for your next gathering. B / $25 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

The Gin Edit Recipe Cards – This deck of recipes looks as if it took a wrong turn out of a coffee table book and gloriously landed on your bar cart or shelf. Which is exactly the right wrong turn to take. And it’s the sort of artwork that makes the deck function as genuine décor before even mixing a single drink: the rare cocktail accessory justifying itself aesthetically, even during the stretches when not being used. Inside The Gin Edit are fifty recipes across four categories: fizzes/spritzes, classics, modern and drinks with a twist. They’re all arranged with enough logic that a reasonably bright person should be able to follow both the user experience and recipes with minimal fuss. The first three categories are quite approachable, but the final one, “with a twist”, earns its name. Newcomers should approach those cards with interest, but also a realistic assessment of one’s current abilities. A- / $25 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

title: Review: Compass Box Brulee Royale
summary:
Compass Box prides itself on delivering elaborate Scotch blends that are unique not just for their quality but the way in which they often reflect a place or theme, or in the case of Brûlée Royale, a food. In their telling, they are not blenders, but “whiskymakers” because their whiskies are “deliberately imagined.” This latest…

The post Review: Compass Box Brulee Royale appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Compass Box prides itself on delivering elaborate Scotch blends that are unique not just for their quality but the way in which they often reflect a place or theme, or in the case of Brûlée Royale, a food. In their telling, they are not blenders, but “whiskymakers” because their whiskies are “deliberately imagined.” This latest limited edition certainly shows some imagination, although the blend itself is not nearly as complicated as some past Compass Box releases.

Launched in late 2025, Brûlée Royale was inspired by crème brûlée, the iconic French dessert created by Francois Massiolot in the 17th century kitchens of Versailles. Compass Box blender Samuel Travers blended just four component whiskies for this creation, all with a focus on the sweetening influence of toasted and charred American oak. A large chunk of the blend (39%) comes from a slightly older parcel of the same Clynelish single malt used to deliver a bold sweetness in the brand’s core Nectarosity release. The majority (53.3%), however, is 18-year-old Benrinnes aged in first-fill barrels that reportedly helped contribute a creamy texture, while the remainder comprises 24-year-old Speyburn aged in refill hogsheads (7.2%) and barely a whiff of 23-year-old Ardbeg (0.5%) aged in re-charred casks. On paper, it sounds like a pretty rich dram, but is it actually the dessert course that its name suggests?

Compass Box Brulée Royale Review

The aroma is instantly sweet with honeyed notes of spun sugar and buttercream. It’s never cloying, however, with the malt delivering a grounding foundation of nougatine and buttery pastry dough complimented by the gentle waxiness of the Clynelish. A bit of orchard fruit flickers in and out, trying to give form to all that airy sweetness, but notes of baked pear and dried citrus peels are short-lived, giving way to more caramelized sugars and toffees. With more time in the glass, fresh cut oak and a hint of minerality add more subtle contrast to this whisky’s sweeter designs.

On the palate, the bakery steals the show with early notes of crème caramel and vanilla icing, warm apple tarts and pecan pralines. The malt once again adds doughiness to the experience, accentuating a pastry-filled midpalate of almond croissants and sugary palmier. That brûléed sugar note, for which the whisky is named, is ever-present but measured, offering just enough decadent sweetness without becoming monotone or overly saccharine. The finish is oily and long with soft baking spice, honeycomb, well-baked apple pie, and a fading hint of candle smoke. If there was ever a dessert dram, this is it.

98 proof.

A- / $160

title: Book Review: Wine & Dine At Home: Easy Recipes & Perfect Pairings
summary:
There have been moments where I have experienced a weird dread while standing in the wine shop, holding a bottle of wine with a name I am most certainly mispronouncing in my head, wondering if it is an insult to the meal I’m about to prepare, and whether or not it’s a reasonable hedge against…

The post Book Review: Wine & Dine At Home: Easy Recipes & Perfect Pairings appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
There have been moments where I have experienced a weird dread while standing in the wine shop, holding a bottle of wine with a name I am most certainly mispronouncing in my head, wondering if it is an insult to the meal I’m about to prepare, and whether or not it’s a reasonable hedge against humiliating myself with the soon-to-be assembled dinner party. It’s not a wine problem, really, but a confidence issue. It’s exactly the sort of problem Charlotte Kristensen’s Wine & Dine at Home aims to solve.

The book’s structure is the first clue that someone in charge understands how humans behave, which is to say: poorly, constantly under deadline pressure, with strongly held opinions on garlic and newly formed opinions about soccer. The book is arranged in three movements: Discover, Pair and Curate. This may sound like an agenda for a forced corporate retreat but in practice, it is a very forgiving syllabus. “Discover” lays out the fundamentals of food and wine pairing without intimidating the novice reader wishing to learn more. “Pairing” gets down to the nitty-gritty, with fifty wines and recipes varying in complexity: you should definitely have more than a passing knowledge of how to make a meal that isn’t one involving a microwave. However, there’s a section for those culinarily deficient later in the book (more on that in a second). Finally, “Curate” zooms out into thematic, full-course menus for the rare and blessed occasion people are arriving at your house on purpose. There’s also a quick detour into “Takeout Night,” providing those who are not quite up to snuff in the kitchen yet with a quick and easy alternative, and also hopefully avoiding the risk of food illness from something being undercooked.

One of the things that makes Wine & Dine tick so well, and gives it a bit of distinction, is that Kristensen writes like someone who actually wants you to enjoy your dinner, not just survive it. She refuses to give in to the practice of treating wine pairing as if it is some code to be cracked by people with excess disposable income. There’s an unpretentious joy running throughout. There’s zero interest in making the reader feel bad that they’ve been pairing anything and everything with Pinot Grigio out of habit; Kristensen is more interested in showing the reader that there might be something interesting going on one aisle and two shelves over, and that “more interesting” is a perfectly suitable reason to try something. That is a wildly countercultural position in a world of wine writing focused around the principle that pleasure must be earned through toil, suffering and a working knowledge of the soil composition in the mountains of Mendoza.

The pairing logic is explained, rather than declared as gospel. This matters because the entire proposition of this book is to teach the reader how to reason their way to a decent bottle at the shop or supermarket, while this book stays on the bookshelf or kitchen counter at home. That’s the actual gift here: not the fifty recipes, but the method of generating the 51st and 52nd one on your own, on Thursday evening, with guests arriving in under two hours’ time.

If there’s a drawback here, it’s the same uniform complaint that could be made about any genuinely good hosting book, which is that it can make the reader feel more ambitious than the actual kitchen, schedule, budget or skill can comfortably support. And you may find yourself building a five-course evening centered around right-bank Bordeaux for what was supposed to be burger night with one other person. But that’s really not a flaw, either. It’s an unlisted side effect of enthusiasm that is transmitted with success, which is the entire job of this sort of book.

This is the kicker making Wine & Dine succeed at the only task that matters for a book of this style: it makes you want to go buy a bottle of something you’ve never tried before and cook it next to something tonight for no particular reason other than just to see what happens. That’s not just wine education, that’s a good time. Just organized in a slightly more intelligent fashion than usual.

A- / $27 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

content:
Perched atop a hill in upstate New York, five miles outside Hudson and 117 miles from New York City, sits a future center of the American brandy industry. In time, it could well become the nation’s premier producer of fine fruit spirits, with products to rival the age, complexity, and pedigree of those most European expressions.

Of course, “could” is an important qualifier, and that’s if everything goes well. It will take generations to turn this slice of the Hudson Valley into one of the world’s great brandy regions. Fortunately for Klocke Estate, its founder John Frishkopf is comfortable planning centuries ahead.

What started as a daydream has steadily evolved into a remarkable and unique operation. Nearly 20 years after Frishkopf was first inspired by European spirits, Klocke is just a handful of years into operations. Yet it’s already producing some of the most exciting spirits in its region — and its long-term goals are some of the nation’s most aspirational. Simultaneously, Klocke has built a hospitality program poised to make the leap from hidden gem to true destination.

Earlier this year, I visited Klocke to get a firsthand look at what Frishkopf and team are building — and how they’re balancing near term goals with 200 year ambitions.

European Origins and Hudson Valley Roots

In his early career, John Frishkopf didn’t imagine a future in spirits. Instead, the MIT graduate pursued professions in finance, technology, and infrastructure. Those focuses took him to Europe, where he worked for a decade across Vienna, London, and Prague. But it wasn’t long before Frishkopf caught the brandy bug, inspired by European hospitality and after-dinner tastings with friends and found family.

Born with a tinkerer’s mindset, he eventually began experimenting with home distillation. Upon returning to America, spirits, and Frishkopf was soon disheartened by the relative paucity of home-grown brandy options. America was quickly becoming even more whiskey-obsessed, and domestic brandy almost felt like an afterthought, relegated to the realm spirits nerds of and small-yet-passionate producers. The nation, it seemed, lacked a signature style with clout to rival spirits Cognac, Armagnac, and Calvados. Changing that would require establishing strong roots — both literally and figuratively — while thinking hundreds of years forward.

Starting in 2008, Frishkopf began quietly exploring regions and properties to build a new style of American brandies. That dream stayed on hold until around 2016, when he retired from his day job and began searching in earnest for the perfect property. The search took him across the country, and for a time, New England looked like a prime candidate.

Eventually, he settled on the Hudson Valley and Finger Lakes. The region’s soil and climate lend themselves to apples and grapes with high acidity and relatively low sugar content. Winemakers might see that as a challenge. But Frishkopf believes the region — and importantly, its fruit — is uniquely suited to growing both world class apples and grapes for distillate.

In early 2018, Frishkopf acquired roughly 160 acres of former farmland in Claverack, New York. From there, Frishkopf and his team began construction on what he calls an “earth-to-glass” brandy distillery, farm, and hospitality center. Executing on his 200-year, multi-generational business plan, however, would prove easier said than done.

Building Klocke

Frishkopf initially self-funded Klocke’s buildout before eventually raising outside capital from local investors, in addition to grants and tax incentives. Early steps included parsing the property, of which about 90 acres are cultivable. Heavy clay soil required an extensive drainage project, and teams installed more than 33 miles of drainage tile. Roads, paths, and terraces had to be carved anew.

Along the way, Frishkopf’s team looked for every opportunity to maximize sustainability. Cleared underbrush was turned into literal tons of biochar, a boon to soil health and drainage. The company believes it’s the first operation in the state to use this technique with locally harvested plant waste.

By 2020, the estate’s first plots were ready for planting. Orchards currently boast 43 cider apple varieties across bittersweets, bittersharps, and sweets; vineyards focus on nine types of grape.

Cultivation is one part of the equation, and distillation is another. Klocke purchased two main stills for production. For aged spirits, Klocke bought a 2,500-liter, direct-fired (via propane) Alembic Charentais pot still imported from Cognac. For unaged spirits, it commissioned a custom 500-liter Müller copper still from Oberkirch, Germany. The property also features a French-style Chai (or barrel cellar) constructed with timber framing, two-foot-tick straw bale walls, and a natural clay floor.

Progressing from Frishkopf’s daydream to full-scale operation has also meant growing the team. Klocke currently employs around 15 people across management and production, alongside four seasonal employees and nearly 40 hospitality staff.

Klocke’s Spirits Program

It will take decades to realize Frishkopf’s dream of multi-decade age statements. In the meantime, Klocke certainly isn’t sitting idle, and its portfolio is growing at a pre-planned, steady clip. Klocke’s first apple brandy was distilled in 2022, with cider from the 2021 harvest. With the current setup, production in the Alembic Charentais still takes around 11 hours, with three initial distillations feeding a secondary distillation.

In late 2024, Klocke released its first unoaked brandy, dubbed “00 Apple Brandy.” Its first aged, oaked product — Referent Apple Brandy — followed roughly a year later with 400 bottle limited release. Meanwhile, the estate’s early distillates continue to age in the Chai, primarily in French limousine casks. While the company hasn’t divulged its exact schedule, it’s likely we’ll see gradually older apple (and eventually grape-based) releases in the coming years.

Klocke is also leveraging its Müller still for eaux de vie made with fruit from local sourcing partners. Early releases have included spirits distilled from plum, sour cherry, and Traminette grapes. Klocke also currently produces lines of vermouth, liqueurs, and ready-to-drink cocktails, marketed as complements to the growing brandy portfolio.

On the weekend I visited, Klocke had just begun experimenting with a grappa-style brandy. That particular project, it seems, is still somewhat under wraps. Team members wanted time to assess and adjust before offering outsiders like me a taste.

Hudson Valley Hospitality

In Frishkopf’s mind, the foundation for a new, world-class spirits category doesn’t rest on bottles alone. He’s long envisioned Klocke as a multifaceted destination, where visitors to the Hudson Valley can tour the grounds and production while sipping and eating to their heart’s content. Attached to the distillery is an expansive bar and restaurant, with interior design by Ken Fulk.

Both were unveiled during Klocke’s July 2024 grand opening. The food menu is seasonal, curated, and often portioned for sharing. And while the wine menu is expansive, food is even complemented by a select cocktail menu and offering of house pours, in addition to spirit-free options.

Currently, Klocke Estate offers a 30 minute distillery tour and tasting, in addition to a Brandy 101 workshop and farm tour. In the future, Frishkopf envisions expanding tour offerings that may include barrel tastings/cask selections, in addition to more hands-on explorations of Klocke’s brandymaking process. Those experiences could give visitors deep insight into how Klocke’s house style evolves from harvest to harvest and year to year.

In an ideal world, Klocke’s farm, spirits, and hospitality programs will interweave as an ecosystem, designed to be explored on-sight and then captured in bottlings to export far and wide. As with any finely aged brandy, it will be a long and sometimes unpredictable process; from the field to the barrel, nature must necessarily run its course. But Frishkopf is quick to emphasize he isn’t just building for the here and now. It’s that very patience — and persistence — that could lead to success over the road ahead.
